Fifteen Strips

Colorimeter XCN-001  ·  pad analysis  ·  13 August 2026

Fifteen Strips

The instrument now measures a reagent pad to about one percent. Two strips prepared at the same concentration still disagree by a factor of two. The splash is not what did it.

15 captures · 13 exposed strips · 2 unexposed 5–256 ppb nominal Ascel 458201, lot 0 12V601-HH reports 9–13

Instrument

0.83 %

Spread of the strip's own bare paper across fifteen strips, two stages and four days. Median cell; worst 1.21 %.

Chemistry

1.6–1.9×

Spread in the concentration read back from strips prepared at one nominal value — 16 to 38 times the instrument's contribution.

Splash hypothesis

Not supported

A droplet leaves a local mark. The disagreement is in the pad's overall level, and the shielded and unshielded groups overlap.

What was asked

The question, and what the data can answer

You suspected that some of the earlier strips were sprayed with stray droplets during the reaction, and collected thirteen more — four of them shielded — to find out.

The set does answer whether a droplet landed on a pad, because a droplet is a local event and the images resolve about a fifth of a millimetre. It does not answer whether shielding helps, because every shielded strip was run on one day and every unshielded strip on another, and the stage was repainted and two illuminants switched off in between. That confound is stated plainly rather than papered over.

What the set does answer, and did not set out to, is how reproducible the assay is at all, how the colour grows with concentration, and where the useful range ends. Those are the substantive findings.

One capture is missing

C1001, at 76 ppb, has no archive in captures/. It is absent from every table below. If it exists elsewhere, add the file and one row to samples.py and re-run.

Finding 1 · report9

The instrument is not the limiting term

Every claim about the strips rests on the photometry being reproducible, so it is tested first on quantities that carry no chemistry at all.

The bare paper below the pad is the same material on every strip and carries no reagent. Measured through the fitted illumination surface against the two gray chips, it reads the same on all fifteen captures — 0.83 % standard deviation for the median cell, 1.21 % for the worst — across fifteen different strips, two stages, and four days. A reflectance also has to be independent of exposure time, and the two hundred and eighteen cells measured on more than one rung agree to a median of 0.25 %.

The two strips photographed before use put a floor under the blank correction: their unexposed pads disagree by 0.0021 absorbance. On the fitted dose-response that is about 2.5 ppb at three standard deviations — the smallest concentration the optics alone would allow — 3.2 ppb at three standard deviations.

Evidence · report9.py — exposure consistency, bare-paper reflectance across the inventory, the two unexposed pads.
Caveat · the blank floor rests on two unexposed pads only.

Finding 2 · report10

The colour grows as the square of concentration, then stops

Each strip reduces to dA: the absorbance of its pad measured against its own bare paper a few millimetres away, less the absorbance an unexposed pad shows for the same reason. Referring the pad to its own substrate rather than to the gray card cancels the card, the lamp, and everything that changed between one session's stage and the next's.

Over the strips at 32 ppb and below the response fits

dA = 6.62 × 10−4 · ppb1.80

— markedly super-linear. Doubling the concentration more than triples the colour. Whatever the mechanism, it means sensitivity collapses at the low end: the difference between 5 and 10 ppb is a quarter of the difference between 20 and 25.

Above about 32 ppb it stops. At 256 ppb the pad develops one twentieth of the absorbance the low-range law predicts, and the 128 and 256 ppb strips differ by less than two strips prepared at 16 do. The useful window on this lot is roughly 5 to 30 ppb; above that the strip records that the concentration is high and little more.

Finding 3 · report10

Replicates disagree by about a factor of two

Three concentrations carry replicates. Converting each strip's absorbance back through the fitted curve gives the concentration the instrument would report for it:

prepared atstripsread back asspread
5 ppbC1011, C10123.7  ·  6.31.7×
16 ppbC1008, C1009, C101012.4  ·  16.9  ·  23.21.9×
64 ppbC1004, C1005, C100626.4  ·  37.2  ·  41.61.6×

The 16 ppb group is the cleanest test — three strips, and its widest pair sits on the same day with the same operator, the same stage and the same reagents. They differ by 1.9×. That is the number to design against: a single strip locates a concentration to roughly a factor of two. The instrument and the blank together come to 0.0042 absorbance; the scatter between the three 16 ppb strips is 0.066, or sixteen times that. At 64 ppb the ratio is thirty-eight.

The exception is the bottom of the range. At 5 ppb the two strips scatter by 0.0082 absorbance, only twice the instrument term — so a quarter of the variance there is photometry, not chemistry, and below about 5 ppb the two become comparable. That is the one place where improving the instrument would still buy accuracy.

The 64 ppb group deserves a caution. It sits in the saturating region where the curve is shallow, so a modest difference in absorbance maps onto a large difference in inferred concentration; and all three read back well below 64. That is the saturation of Finding 2, not three bad strips.

The expired strip

X15 was prepared at 10 ppb and develops dA 0.53 — darker than every strip below 128 ppb in the set, and reading back as 41 ppb. Comparing it cell by cell against C1005 (64 ppb) gives a flat ratio, CV 1.7 %: it is not merely dark, it is the same colour as a 64 ppb strip, so no choice of illuminant or algorithm could separate them. An expired strip does not fail safe.

Evidence · report10.py sections 3 and 4; report8.py for the X15 colour comparison.
Caveat · two strips at 5 ppb, three at 16 and 64. These are ranges, not standard deviations.

Finding 4 · report12

No pad carries a droplet mark

This is the direct test of the splash hypothesis, and it does not depend on the confounded grouping. A droplet is a local event, a fraction of a millimetre across; the pad measures 41.4 × 53.3 layer pixels, which puts one pixel between 0.15 and 0.19 mm. So each pad is separated into three parts — a smooth cubic surface, which absorbs the gradient the reaction itself leaves as the sample wicks through; the pixel-scale granularity left over; and the largest coherent excursion after smoothing at a droplet's scale.

The two unexposed pads set the floor: granularity 0.006 absorbance, no feature above 1.6 times it. Nothing in the optics or the paper puts a mark on a pad.

Across the eleven strips that developed a usable colour, the granularity is 7.0 ± 2.5 % of the dye absorbance — a constant relative roughness from 10 to 256 ppb. The dye is laid down with a fixed grain, not with a fixed noise. And the largest coherent feature in each pad, measured against that pad's own granularity, runs from 1.4 to 2.2 for ten of the eleven. The shielded strips are not the quiet ones — they span 1.4 to 2.0, the unshielded 1.6 to 3.7, and the two groups overlap almost entirely.

One capture stands clear. C1003, at 128 ppb and unshielded, carries a compact, sharply bounded lighter patch near the upper right of its pad at 3.7 times its granularity, and about five pixels across — of order a millimetre, and quite unlike the diffuse mottling everywhere else. That is what a droplet mark would look like. It is one capture out of thirteen, it lightens rather than darkens the pad, and removing it changes nothing about the conclusions above.

What this rules out

Whatever makes two strips at 16 ppb differ by 1.9×, it is not a droplet landing on one of them. The disagreement is in the pad's overall level, uniform across its area, and the shielded strips show it as clearly as the unshielded.

Evidence · report12.py — trend, granularity and largest coherent feature, per pad, against the two unexposed controls.

Finding 5 · report13

An uncontrolled step in the protocol tracks the scatter

Each archive stores the reaction's timing. Both reagent periods are held to a second across the whole set — 120–121 s and 420–421 s. Two intervals are not controlled at all: the gap between reagent 1 finishing and reagent 2 starting ran from 20 to 157 seconds, and the wait before the capture from 38 to 87.

Tested against the residuals about the low-range curve, the gap is the one that tracks them: r = −0.82, permutation p = 0.019, explaining 68 % of the residual variance. Its sign says a longer gap gives a weaker colour, which is chemically reasonable — the reduced arsenic species has longer to be lost before the zinc goes in.

Read this as a direction, not a result

Seven strips in the low range, and six quantities were examined, so the p value to judge it by is nearer 0.11 than 0.02. No strip was run at a deliberately different gap. The way to settle it is a set in which the gap is varied on purpose at one concentration with everything else held — which is cheap, and is the single most valuable thing to collect next.

Nothing else came close: the wait before capture gave r = −0.30, sample temperature +0.43, both consistent with chance at this sample size.

Evidence · report13.py — permutation tests over every recorded interval, with the shielding/session confound tabulated.

Finding 6 · report11

Photographing the strip first is worth doing

C1010 and C1011 were each imaged twice, before and after exposure, with the strip taken out of the stage in between. Two independent placements of one physical object.

The strip's own bare paper repeats to a median 0.43 % between the two placements, worst 1.54 % — the whole chain, placement included, measured on one unchanging surface. The fitted geometry repeats to 0.15 px in width and 0.5° in tilt for C1010. C1011 moved 8.25 px up the channel between placements, far enough that the stage mask hid the top of its pad; the finder detects that and drops the hidden rows.

Using each strip's own blank rather than the average of both shifts its dye absorbance by 0.0025 — about 14 % of the signal at 5 ppb, and under 3 % at 16. So a per-strip blank matters near the detection limit and is unnecessary above roughly 10 ppb. Given that a pre-exposure image costs one capture cycle, it is worth taking at the low end.

Evidence · report11.py — placement repeatability, own blank versus shared, and the resolution floor.

Instrument note

The black paint did what you hoped

Painting the surround flat black more than halved the width of the strip's edge transition. On the original stage the 20–80 % transition had a median width of 3.57 layer px and ran as wide as 8.2; on the repainted stage the median is 1.49 px and the worst is 3.8. Two edges on the old stage had no dark surround beside them at all — the channel wall was lit — and could not be measured.

That matters because a soft edge does not merely blur, it displaces: the half-level crossing moves inward and the strip measures narrower than it is. All six captures whose edges are sharp enough to contribute to the pooled width are on the repainted stage. The pooled width, 41.35 ± 0.24 px, agrees with the 41.11 ± 0.21 published from the earlier set by a different method — an independent confirmation of both.

Two things the new captures broke, and how the tools handle them

The 13 August captures have no white illuminant, and the pad finder read B/G under white light. It now works on a composite reflectance — every stored illuminant × layer, each divided by its own gray-chip level, then averaged. That is nearly dye-blind, so the pad's edges appear as physical features rather than chemical ones, and the finder no longer cares which illuminants a capture holds.

The pad's ends were found from a colour step down the strip, which does not exist on an unexposed or very faint pad. The lower edge is now taken from the pad's own shadow line — present whatever the colour — and the top placed one pad-height above it. Where the top can still be measured directly, on thirteen of fifteen captures, it agrees to 0.39 px r.m.s.

A defect worth knowing about

The bare paper is about twice as bright as the gray chips, so on the blue and royal-blue cells it reaches the sensor ceiling a rung or two before the pad and the chips do. Averaging a clipped rung into the paper reference produced an apparent 9.5 % session-to-session drift in royal_blue.B that does not exist. measure.py now screens the paper separately and nulls its value on the rungs where it clipped.

Evidence · padrect.py run directly prints the geometry line for every capture; report7.py draws the rectangles.

Limits

What this set cannot tell you

  • Whether shielding helps. Shielding, session, stage and illuminant set move together. Nothing here can attribute a difference between the groups to any one of them. Run shielded and unshielded strips alternately in one session and the question becomes answerable in an afternoon.
  • Whether the nominal concentrations are right. The dose-response exponent of 1.80 is real in the sense that the data show it, but a systematic error in the dilution series at the low end would produce the same curvature. An independently verified standard at 5 and at 25 ppb would separate the two.
  • Anything about a blank. There is no 0 ppb strip taken through the full reaction. The unexposed pads are not the same thing: they never met reagent 1 or reagent 2. A true reagent blank is the missing control.
  • Whether the assay drifts within a session. Every replicate group except 16 ppb spans sessions.

One thing that is settled, and was already suspected: extra illuminants buy nothing. Over the nine captures that carry all ten, a rank-one model — one spectral shape scaled by a per-strip dye loading — captures 90.6 % of the between-strip variance. The four short-wavelength cells (cyan.Gb, blue.Gb, cyan.B, blue.B) resolve about 200 times the blank disagreement; the amber and red cells resolve essentially nothing and are references.

Next

What to collect, in order of value

  1. Vary the reagent gap on purpose. Six strips at one concentration — say 25 ppb, in the middle of the useful window — at gaps of 20, 40, 60, 80, 100 and 120 s, everything else held. This either confirms Finding 5 or kills it, and it is one afternoon.
  2. Run a reagent blank. Deionised water through the full protocol. Without it the bottom of the curve is unanchored.
  3. Alternate shielded and unshielded within one session. Four of each, at 25 ppb, interleaved. That breaks the confound the current set carries.
  4. Replicates at one concentration, n ≥ 5. The factor-of-two figure rests on ranges of two and three strips. Five would give it a standard deviation.
  5. Stop collecting above 30 ppb for calibration purposes. Those strips cost the same and carry almost no information about concentration. If the high range matters, dilute the sample instead.

Two smaller things: photograph the strip before exposure whenever working below 10 ppb, and keep the strip clear of the channel walls — C1005 sat at −2.0° and C1013's left edge was in a wall's shadow.

Reproducing this

Every number above, from the archives

Full instructions are in desktop/padanalysis/HOWTO.md. The short version:

cd ~/Projects/Colorimeter
.venv/bin/python3 desktop/padanalysis/measure.py 6 rect
for n in 9 10 11 12 13; do
    .venv/bin/python3 desktop/padanalysis/report$n.py
done

The first command writes records.json; each report prints its findings and writes a figure into fig/. To add a strip, drop the archive into captures/ and add one row to samples.py. To check the pad finder before trusting anything, run padrect.py directly and read the soft, clr and rms columns. To confirm nothing depends on how much pad edge is discarded, run sweep.py.

Everything is read-only against captures/ and src/colorimeter.sqlite.
